translations.text: I praise you, brothers, because you have not merely devoted yourselves to hearing the words, but have stored within yourselves the beauty of their meaning. Like a wise bee entering the immortal and spiritual [?] of the holy Scriptures, among these flowers adorned with the blossoms of devotion to God, let each of you make the honey of divine sayings in the hidden beehives of your souls. Just as the nature and strength of bees come from flowers, and their labors produce something to be enjoyed, so the flower and strength of devotion to God come from the divine Scriptures, and the enjoyment of devotion to God comes from the labors of the virtuous. He fashioned within himself such honeycomb-like [?] of divine sayings. And blessed David, having tasted how good devotion to God is, proclaimed and cried out in the melodies of his psalms: “Your words are sweeter to my palate than honey to my mouth.”

Yet I do not praise your eagerness so much as I marvel at our father’s freedom from envy. He blossoms with divine love and shines with heavenly gifts; he waters the Church so abundantly and in such a manner, and gladdens this city of God. It is timely to speak the words of the psalm: “The streams of the river gladden the city of God.” He pours forth such holy and clear streams, yet does not disdain the few drops of our words. Such a cloud, laden with heavenly rain, does not hesitate to receive the little patter of our tongue, but joins you in praising it. Before you do so, through the intercession of his holy prayers, he grants us speakers the ability to speak and the listeners the eagerness to listen. And he praises what is his own as though it belonged to another, imitating his Lord, Christ, who received what came from the prophets and praised the prophet’s proclamation. He himself spoke through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah, and he himself made the inspiration of the Holy Spirit resound. Yet, receiving his own words as though they came from the prophet, he says to the Jews: “Hypocrites, Isaiah spoke well about you.” It was not Isaiah who spoke well, but you who spoke well through Isaiah—and through all the prophets. Zechariah bears witness: “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets.” It was not the mouths of the prophets, but the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Just as a reed pen writes not what it wishes, but what the hand directs, so the tongue of the prophets spoke not what it wished, but what the abundance of the Holy Spirit commanded. For this reason they rightly consider David’s cry beautiful: “My tongue is like the pen of a swift writer.”

And now our admirable father himself, through his holy prayers, will grant us an abundance of speech; what his prayers give, he himself hears and praises. Now, since we have such a father, and the feast is just beginning, come: supported by his holy prayers, let us take flight to the height of the glory of the Only-Begotten and raise our minds. Not that we can attain any comprehension of the greatness of his honor, but let us eagerly seek to reach him in love. For nothing can comprehend the honor of the Only-Begotten: neither the breadth of words nor the capacities of minds. He surpasses—surpasses every mind and every thought. Blessed David expressed this figuratively when he said: “A person will approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted.” The more someone reflects upon words about God, the higher above him he finds the knowledge of the truth.

And now let us speak of the goodness of the Only-begotten in the present reading. The fountain of wisdom uses parables—the one who spoke through David’s mouth, saying, “I will open my mouth in parables.” He gives an example and a parable full of power, though, judging by its words, it seems to bear no resemblance to his goodness. “Which of you has a friend and goes to him at midnight and says, ‘Friend, give me three loaves of bread, because a friend of mine has arrived from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’? And he answers and says, ‘The doors are shut, and my children are with me in bed. Do not trouble me. I cannot get up and give you anything.’” And what follows this? “Truly I tell you, even if he will not give to him because of their friendship, nevertheless, because of his persistence, he will get up and give him more than he wanted. And I tell you: ask, and you will receive.” What resemblance does the parable bear to his goodness? For he is sleepless by nature, while this man lies idle in bed. He is not overcome by sluggishness, while this man is a slave to sluggishness and sleep. Now what corresponding resemblance does the parable intend to show? He adds to this, “You too must ask,” just as that man persisted in asking the sleeper. Surely you do not sleep too? Did not the prophets cry out concerning you, “The guardian of Israel neither dozes nor sleeps”? Now what corresponding resemblance does your parable intend to make clear?

The words of the Life-giver customarily present likenesses through similar things and show the opposite through contrary things. He makes this clear in another parable as well. When he wished to demonstrate his overflowing goodness, his abundant and abounding gifts, and his inexhaustible generosity by means of a contrast, he introduced an example like the one we have just heard. But first let this be examined, so that what he intends to show may become clear. Although the example is not similar, the Savior means to say that the petitioner persuaded the man who was enslaved to sleep, beset by sluggishness, and disheartened behind his closed doors to persevere and satisfy [?], and through his persistence overcame his irritation. Will he not persuade the nature that is free from sluggishness—I mean the one who is neither affected by irritation nor enslaved to sleep—to persevere and satisfy [?] for those who truly approach him? And who would take up arms and fight against such reasoning? So that you may learn with certainty that he taught the opposite through a contrast, he proceeds a little further down and uses the same kind of example to show the opposite through a contrast: “Which of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? And if he asks for a fish, will he give him a snake instead of a fish? And if he asks for an egg, will he give him a scorpion instead of an egg?” After speaking of better things by comparison with human conduct, he then says, “If you, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father, the heavenly Father, give good things to those who ask him!” Do you see how he showed the opposite by comparison with its contrary?

He also uses another parable of this kind elsewhere, as I have already said. I consider it important to explain what it is and what force it has. “There was a judge,” he says, “in a certain city, who neither feared God nor felt shame before people. A widow continually persisted in pleading with him, but he never settled her case. Because of his harshness and his failure to acknowledge God, he would not yield to her pleading appeals. But her persistence overcame his cruel harshness. The unjust judge said to himself, ‘Though I do not fear God or feel shame before people, nevertheless, because she is wearing me out, I will give her justice.’” This is the parable he tells. But the Savior wished to show the opposite by contrasting it with this, and immediately added: “See,” he says, “what the unjust judge said.” If the widow’s persistence, endurance, and insistence brought the unjust and cruel man to agreement [?], will not the persistence and endurance of those who continue pleading move the gentle and abundantly compassionate Father, the Lord who loves humankind, to hear their appeals and show mercy? He showed this through that parable, and he speaks of the same thing now: “And I tell you: ask, and you will receive; knock, and it will be opened to you.” Follow the example of the friend who knocked at the door and said, “Friend, open to me.” You too must knock, and it will be opened. Seek, and you will find.

But now let us bring our discourse to this point, for I know that this is precisely what you were asking for, and I see you crowded together, cramped, and eager to hear the discourse. But take comfort, for Isaiah has come and will give you encouragement: “Be at ease amid your cramped conditions, you who are eager to listen.” He spoke well; listen well, all of you, though cramped, with your spirits enlarged and at ease, so that your discomfort here may bring you relief from many afflictions. Those who endure sweat upon their bodies for God’s sake dispel all the pains of sin. For if sweat produced by the body dispels pains, will not such sweat as pours out for God’s sake and for the sake of his words, from the fountain of the longing with which you have come to listen, surely wash away all sins at once?

But let us turn to the matter before us, for I know that you are asking for the remainder of the discourse. Many eagerly ask for it as friends would, while many hunt for grounds of complaint and think of finding fault. For the criticism of the many who wish to find fault with us has not escaped us: they say that we left the subject unexamined because of some inability. But I am astonished at such people, not at their accusations, but at their bad timing. You blame me as though you had made a loan and had not received repayment. When you asked for the explanation, was I [?] from resolving it? Did someone else put the question before me, and did I reject it? I made the promise myself, and I myself forgot. If that is so, blame the weaknesses of my nature, and do not criticize the account given in the discourse. For even if the [?] escaped us, still the weakness of the discourse would not destroy the force of the question. The claims of truth are not driven into exile by my inability, for the reasons for the matters before us are indeed evident. But the abundance of the words I have spoken tossed my thoughts this way and that, drawing them away from the question before us. And now I will willingly discharge the debt of what I then left unfinished unwillingly.

Even when I repay it, I hesitate again, because I see in you a new and wonderful kind of drunkenness: a drunkenness that does not bring the mind into a stupor, but stimulates recollection more and more. You all know that drunkenness makes the mind senseless. But you, brothers, the more you become drunk on the divine word, the more you drive away mental stupor and plant divine recollections in its place. This is precisely what is remarkable: the drunken cupbearers become weighed down by their excessive service, while you, who have drained so many vessels of the divine word, are thirsty even after becoming drunk, and insistently ask for what remains. Truly, one gets to hear the words of those who are spiritually drunk. “What is the cup?” they say. “The cup remains. He did not explain the cup; he did not discharge his debt concerning the words about the cup.” I love you for longing for Christ’s cup. I love you for asking for what remains. I love you for not wanting to lose even one cup of this beautiful drunkenness. And you are entirely right. At a bodily feast, someone who passes over a single cup out of moderation is admirable. But in divine rejoicing and at the heavenly table, someone who allows none of the things that lead to drunken dissipation, but instead finds refreshment and grows hungry, becomes drunk and grows thirsty all at once—this is the person who will truly be satisfied with eternal salvation. And now I call both speakers and hearers blessed: you hearers, because you thirst to hear, just as the Savior says, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied”; and the speakers, because they make divine teaching resound in attentive ears. Blessed are those who speak into the ears of those who listen. Now let us come to the words.

“Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” These words are full of questions and stir up many violent passions among the heretics—not because anything wrong has been said, but because they badly misunderstand the phrase “if it is possible.” Some imagined an infallible decree that cannot be transgressed, [?] from the flesh: that is, fate, allotment, and the necessity of what is mythically called nativity, as though something were thus allotted to each person from birth. Others dishonor the dignity of the Only-begotten in another way: they attach a slavish obedience to the Son in relation to the Father. “He was under the Father’s authority,” they say, “and that is why he offered such supplications.” What explanation is suitable for us to resolve these questions? What understanding will suffice to unravel the many-voiced fables of the heretics? We cannot [?] learn from any other source than the truth itself. Come, then, let us ascend to the divine heights, to the saving plan of the Life-giver above, who does everything and speaks all his words not only in accordance with the dignity proper to him, but also in accordance with the saving plan suited to us. To put it briefly—for I always like to speak concisely and express much in few words—the Life-giver knew beforehand that the sufferings were absolutely necessary. He knew beforehand that the cross was being established for the salvation of the world, that death was being rebuked, and that the resurrection was being brought about. He knew this so well that he told the disciples beforehand, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. They will scourge him and crucify him, and on the third day he will rise.”

This is the utterance of God, who knows beforehand what is to come; of God, who anticipates events before they are experienced; of God, who governs human affairs with knowledge. In response to this, Peter again speaks to him, [?], showing concern for his body: “Far be it from you, Lord,” he says. “This must not happen to you.” And how does the Savior respond? He grows angry at this untimely pity and rebukes this misplaced concern: “Get behind me, Satan, for you are thinking not of the things of God, but of the things of men.” Approach the saying rightly. Examine it yourself and keep watch over it, for if you serve the words alone, you will undermine much concerning the Savior: you will accuse him not only of weakness, but also of instability in his thoughts.

O benevolent Lord, when Peter wished that you should not go to the cross, saying, “Far be it from you,” you rebuked him. And now do you yourself ask for the very thing for which you blamed him, something unworthy not only of [?], but even of a steadfast man? Who praises a general who promises a great deal before the battle and boasts against the enemy with great confidence, but turns to flight amid the clash of battle and dishonors his strength through cowardice? Before Christ came to his sufferings, he said to the one who sought to spare him those sufferings: “Get away from me, Satan, for you are thinking not of the things of God, but of the things of men.” Would he who considered such thoughts unworthy of God now adopt the same thoughts himself and pray for that very thing? Oh, the foolishness—or rather, the arrogance—of those who serve the words alone, recklessly venture everything, and dare to interpret divine things in contradictory ways! They refuse to recognize that by accepting the words alone, they portray him not only as lower than the Father, as they are eager to do, but also as inferior to many wise and righteous people, and as entirely lacking human steadfastness.

What wise or righteous person, or anyone at all among mankind whose courage has been attested, would disown his own virtue and dishonor the strength he had promised and previously boasted of? Who would be so cowardly and ill-timed as to venture and undertake one thing, but think another, and shrink from the actual test? He who threatened death with death and proclaimed the good news of the resurrection—how could he himself shrink from the cross? I have said all this to rebuke those who serve the words, dishonor the Lord, and sell the truth. And now, what can one seek to make clear in the face of the contradiction between the words, when the truth is always found consistent with itself? And how can the consistency of the truth be understood at all amid the conflict of words? The words do indeed conflict with one another, but the harmony of the divine utterances stands firm and enduring. Now it is my duty to explain the solution to the question before us with diligent care, and yours to listen with minds eager to learn.

When the Lord drew near to his crucifixion, to complete the whole work of salvation, the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, knew beforehand that many heretics would rise against the truth, would separate the divine sufferings from him, and would falsely declare his deeds alien to him. Especially would this be done by those who bear the name of error—I mean the disciples of the Manichaeans, who even dared to say that Christ’s sufferings were merely a shadow and an illusion before the eyes, as though he had not actually taken a body, and the cross was only an appearance, and his body was merely a shadow and a likeness, and everything accomplished was only an appearance, a shadow, and an illusion before the eyes. Because of such heretical error—I mean that of the disciples of the Manichaeans—and in order to silence the mouths of the heretics beforehand and make it clear that he had put on this body, which is subject to many needs, which recoils from suffering, which trembles at the violence of death, which is troubled and trembles at the end of life, he says, ‘Now my soul is troubled.’ And again, ‘My soul is sorrowful to the point of death.’ And again, ‘If it is at all possible, Father, let this cup pass from me.’ If these things were a shadow, an illusion before the eyes, and a phantom, why was he troubled? If the things being done were merely appearances, why did he recoil? For no one fears a shadow, nor is anyone troubled by mere appearances.

Would you like me also to demonstrate the truth more firmly from an account of our own? Angels entered Sodom. In appearance they seemed to be men, but by nature they were angels. The Sodomites dared to force them, as though they were men, into filth and shameful violation. Now, what did the angels do? Since they knew that they had no body that could be subjected to violence, they were not troubled. Rather, the angels’ nature remained undisturbed and suffered no turmoil from the storm of bodily passions. But Lot, because he considered them righteous men, was troubled lest they suffer some violence. He pleaded with those who were raging: “I beg you,” he said, “do not sin against these men, because they have come under my roof. I will give you my offspring. Take my daughters and do whatever you wish.” Oh, the fervor of his hospitality! He was willing to give his own in place of others to [?]. Lot was troubled as a man, but the angels’ nature suffered no disturbance. For they came outside with great majesty, and they seized and brought away the one who could suffer violence. Those who raged with such lustful fury—or rather, with godless shamelessness—they struck with blindness. They wandered about all night, looking for the door, but could not find it. For those who used their sight wickedly were rightly and justly blinded.

And why was all this said? There is no connection between the preceding discourse and the present one, except that I wished to show that where there is an appearance, there is no fear, but where there is a real body, there are fear and sorrow. Yet, to make entirely clear why he spoke these words, and to cut off the notions of the heretics and establish the teachings of the truth, the Life-giver says to the apostles, “My spirit is willing, but my flesh is weak.” He attributes the weakness to his own flesh, while you attribute the sufferings to his divinity. But unless you hasten to discover the meaning of the saying, you will indeed be found to have dishonored the Lord. For you establish not only what you suppose—that he offered prayers to the Father, and that the one who prays is lower than the one whom he entreats—but I will say something still clearer: if you are a slave to the words alone, you make him not only lower than the Father, but even inferior to his own apostles. Just as they badly misconstrue the saying, “I speak nothing of myself, but my Father gave me a commandment concerning what I should say and what I should speak,” so they do with this one.

Here let apostolic authority come forward and shut the mouths of the madmen. Paul says, “Concerning virgins, I have no command from the Lord, but I give advice.” This shows that the beliefs of the heretics are indeed utterly corrupt. If Paul has authority to act freely without a command from God, does Christ not have authority to speak without commandments from the Father? Here too, by comparison with apostolic courage, the heretical error is exposed, forcibly asserting [?] that the Lord’s words are far beneath the dignity of an apostle. But, as I have already said many times, if you attend only to the words, nothing more is accomplished. If we accept their meaning, the truth remains unblemished—or rather, we ourselves remain unblemished, for the truth is never [?].

Now, if you pay no attention to the interpretation but attend only to the words, you will find Christ fainthearted and speaking in a way far inferior not only to his own dignity but also to apostolic courage. For Christ says, “Now my soul is troubled.” But when Paul went to the region of Palestine, a prophet named Agabus came there and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt in this way.” When all the brothers tried to stop Paul and begged him not to go to Jerusalem, he answered in words of courage—or rather, he spoke in a spirit of courage and apostleship to those who were trying to hold him back: “What are you doing, weeping and crushing my heart within me? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of Christ.”

Paul speaks with such confidence, such boldness, such freedom [?], and tramples underfoot, scorns, and [?] the terrors of death. Yet Paul’s Lord said, “Now my soul is troubled.” Paul’s heart was being crushed, but was Christ really troubled even in his soul? Paul even boasted in afflictions: “Not only this, but we also boast in afflictions, because we know that afflictions produce endurance.” Yet Christ, Paul’s Lord, said, “My soul is sorrowful even to death.” What resemblance does this bear to boasting? Paul regarded his sufferings as grounds for boasting; but did Christ, who strengthened him, really regard the dispensation as a cause of sorrow?

Consider also Paul's [?] elsewhere, how full of courage they are. Once, while he was staying in the city of Philippi in the land of Macedonia, a great crowd rose against him, and he endured all kinds of bodily torture. After inflicting many blows on him, they threw him into prison and secured his feet in the stocks. But the valiant champion of devotion to God, together with Silas, who was with him, overcame their afflictions through self-control and defeated their torments through courage. The writer of the account aptly indicated this when he said, “At midnight Paul and Silas were praising God.” They suffered and gave thanks; they received blows and offered praise. Notice the precision of the writer of the account. He did not say, “At midnight Paul and Silas offered prayers to God,” but that they offered praise. For prayers may arise from distress of heart, while praise arises from gladness of heart. There they see that the apostles were expressing joy: “At midnight,” he says, “Paul and Silas were praising God.” Praise is a sign of rejoicing souls. The saints, wishing to make their souls' joy apparent, did not offer prayers like people in distress, but offered praise like people whose hearts were at ease. Paul and Silas, who were human by nature, showed courageous spirits amid their torments; yet do you attribute godless words to Christ, who is the king of the saints? Do you take what he said for the sake of his providential care as a means of destroying his honor? Come now, put such thoughts away! Let no one insult holy things; let no one slander the divine words; let no one strive to construct impiety from the words of the giver of life, or regard his saving work as a downfall.

But the listener asks us to explain the sequence: “You have taught well,” he says. “They were indeed words belonging to his saving work. But explain also the meaning of that saving work. Why did he use such words at all? Why did he say, ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass from me’?” Brothers, “If it is possible” introduces no compulsion imposed by decrees, nor the mythical term “birth.” These are not words of cowardice, nor does this accuse the speaker of hesitation. Rather, they were expressions of his saving work as a human being and of his concern for those who would stumble. For he knew that his sufferings could cause many to stumble, especially those who were unaware of the mysteries of his saving work, in keeping with the saying, “We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.” Thus he who orders everything with wisdom, taking on the role of human beings, said, “If it is possible to accomplish the saving work in another way and complete it without death, so that such sufferings may not cause many to stumble—if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

“But you are forcing the meaning of the statement,” they say. “Come, show some testimony that bears witness to the truth that he said this because of human weakness and [?].” If that is so, listen: how was he able, right there, to say to the apostle, “Pray; stay awake”? And when they fell asleep, he rebuked them and said, “Could you not keep watch with me for one hour? Pray, so that you may not enter into temptation.” He did not say, “So that I may not enter,” for it was not that the sufferings would harm him, but that they would cause others to stumble. “Pray, so that you may not enter into temptation.” He did not say, “So that we may not enter,” but, “So that you may not enter.” “I am sparing you; it is not that I wish to save myself from suffering. I know what is to come. I am not ignorant of the plan that is to be fulfilled. I am no novice in the blessing that is to blossom for all humanity. But before the events you will see cause you to stumble, I speak in your words: ‘If it is possible for the sufferings to pass, let them pass.’”

The statement must be repeated twice and three times, to make clear that it is something possible, not some unfailing requirement of nature that cannot be avoided, or an inevitable decree, as some have supposed. And do you wish to know with certainty that there was no compulsion or decree imposed from above upon the giver of life, but that this is his own all-knowing plan, and that he accomplishes everything by his own will? Listen, then, to how the Lord himself had already dispelled the notion of compulsion and revealed the abundance of his own freedom of will. “No one,” he says, “takes my life from me. I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again.” And again: “Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up on the third day.” “And if you have authority, why do you utter such a statement? You say, ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass from me.’” “I say it for your sake, you who are weak, and not for my own sake, for I am mighty and almighty, above and beyond every weakness.”

But why did he call his sufferings a cup? This gives rise to yet another question: why did he call his sufferings a cup? Yes, he says, it is the constant practice of Scripture to call the discipline that comes upon offenders a cup. Pay close attention, and be a wise listener. Do not seize upon the words prematurely, but listen and wait for their meaning, for someone who listens badly may interpret what is said badly. Yet someone who speaks in church should not consider it strange if he suffers slander from those who recklessly venture into groundless accusations. For the apostles were slandered as though they had said something wicked. Listen to Paul, and hear how much slander he endured in his preaching: “Not as we are slandered, and as some report that we say, ‘Let us do evil so that good may come.’ Their condemnation is just.” For those who did not hear accuse us as though they had heard. What they did not hear from the teachers, they bring forward as a slander against the teachers. But let us turn to what lies before us. It is Scripture’s characteristic practice to call the discipline or punishments that come upon sinners a cup. But let no hostile spy immediately pick apart these words and say, “Did Christ also sin, then, so that he should bear the punishments of sinners?” Far be it from us to say that! He owed no punishment at all—away with that! [?] Rather, we were subject to punishment, and for us, who were condemned because of our sins and liable to punishment and torment, he took death upon himself. As Isaiah had already proclaimed and announced, he came to death for us sinners. And that he personally took death upon himself as the punishment for sinners, let the Baptist testify: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world”; and the prophet: “He bears our sins and suffers for us,” and, “Because of the sins of the people he came to death.”

His sufferings are called a cup according to the explanation already given. For this very reason, the blessed David also depicts the vengeance that will come upon sinners, saying: “A cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine, blended; all the sinners of the earth will drink it.” Again, when God himself threatened the nations with punishment, he said to Jeremiah: “Take a cup of blended wine and give it to all the nations and to Jerusalem to drink. Say to them, ‘Drink, become drunk, and fall into a stupor.’” What does “fall into a stupor” mean? That discipline brings many people into a stupor, and often into bewilderment as well, especially when they see the righteous caught up with sinners. Just so, even now people throughout the earth complain: “Why were the priests slaughtered at the altars? Why were the holy virgins handed over to abuse? For what reason were so many and such great evils committed? Why did God not protect his own?” And because such afflictions bring people into a stupor and bewilder their minds, he rightly says, “Drink, become senseless, and give yourselves over to drunken excess.” Again, when the Life-giver spoke beforehand to James and John about his own sufferings, he said, “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” This was instead of saying, “Can you bear the sufferings that I am going to bear?” And they said, “Yes.”

But the blessed David clearly showed elsewhere that death suffered for devotion to God is called a cup: “What shall I give the Lord in return for everything he has given me?” Like a deeply grateful servant, he saw God’s benefits pouring out all around him, and he himself sought to give some small return willingly for those boundless benefits. When a poor man receives a rich man into his home, he becomes anxious about what he can prepare to please the rich man and what he can bring to the table that is worthy of his guest’s dignity. He stands perplexed and says to himself, “What can I find that is worthy of this man? What shall I do? What shall I set before him? How shall I honor him? What sort of meal can I prepare?” Likewise, David, looking at human poverty and the greatness of God’s beneficence, saw that there was nothing worthy that a human being could offer to God. He became anxious and perplexed and uttered these words: “What shall I give the Lord in return? I find nothing worthy of his benefits. What shall I give the Lord in return? What sort of person shall I become? What sacrifices shall I offer? With what [?] shall I win the benefactor’s favor?” When he had exhausted every resource, he found only one thing—and even that was worthy not of God’s beneficence, but of his own willingness: “I will receive the cup of salvation.” What does the cup signify? “If I can,” he says, “endure sufferings for devotion to God, if I am able to die for [?]. I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.” And because the meaning was not clear, but concealed and expressed elliptically, he explains it in the words that follow. After “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord,” he adds, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

Now, what does this saying mean: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass”? Is it not clear that he was speaking of his sufferings? But you already have the answer to your question given above. For by saying, “If it is possible,” he fulfills the human form of the divine dispensation. The same one who said this according to his humanity had previously said according to his almighty divinity, “I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again.” He makes it clear that it was not his divinity that shrank from suffering, but the weakness of his flesh. Again he says, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” It was not that the sufferings would do him any harm, but that they would cause others to stumble. He showed this to the disciples: “Remain in prayer,” he says, “so that you do not enter into temptation.” In another way, too, he hands down to us rules for prayer: we must not insist that God grant everything we request in prayer, but entrust ourselves to him who administers everything wisely. For he also says, “Not as I will, but as you will.” What was fitting for him is also very appropriate for you. When you stand in prayer, do not ask for whatever you yourself want, but entrust yourself to God’s will. When you stand in prayer, you too should say, in imitation of Christ, who humbled himself for your sake, “Not as I will, but as you will, Lord.” Entrust yourself to God’s will. Do not dictate to him, and do not set yourself up as his counselor. “For those who love God,” he says, “everything prospers and works together for their good.” Whatever accords with his will is accomplished, and whatever is outside his will does not come to fruition.

The cup of God’s discipline comes upon sinners as punishment. But Christ’s sufferings were not a punishment, but an act of providential care, for he bore the death of sinners without sin, so that he might save the whole world, which had been condemned under sin. Why, someone asks, should he call death a cup at all? The testimonies of Scripture itself clearly show that punishments and death are called a cup. But why were sufferings called a cup, since a cup bears no resemblance to death? Because the disciplines that come upon us are severe, unbearable, and difficult, the divine Scriptures figuratively call afflictions a cup, to make it clear that God does not torment us like a harsh judge or slaughter us without mercy, but heals our pains like a physician and administers discipline inwardly like a medicine of intensely bitter gall. Thus the saving cup of discipline is bitter to taste but beneficial for healing. These words reveal God as a benefactor, who disciplines through the cup: benevolent like a father, and inflicting pain and punishment like a king. He does not strike like an enemy, but causes pain like a physician. Just as a physician, when he uses an iron instrument and applies cautery to the body, is not fighting against the person but battling the disease, so God, when he brings discipline upon us, does not punish his own creation but cleanses its sins. Have you ever seen a physician put his hand to work out of anger, or apply cautery in a fit of rage, or do anything else of that kind? Even though the physician’s face may seem frightening to the sick person, the physician has the patient’s benefit in mind. And just because the treatment seems frightening to the sufferer, it does not follow that the promise of the physician’s skill is anything frightening.

Thus the blessed Paul, rightly and wonderfully defining discipline, says, “All discipline, for a time, seems to bring not joy but sorrow.” When a wounded person sees the physician intending to cut into the wound, he considers him frightening and flees from him as from an enemy. But when he is healed, he then looks closely at the one from whom he once turned his face when he saw him, and bows down before him. Do we not know that sick people insult physicians because their pains make them angry, and that the physician bears with those who are angry? For he knows that their insults are not deliberate but arise from their pain. But when they recover and prevail, they even pay those whom they had considered cruel. They pay them not under compulsion, but with willing eagerness. In the same way, we now resent afflictions; but when the fruit of those afflictions comes, then we praise our benefactor and say in wonder with David, “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into rest.”

And now he calls afflictions a cup—not simply a cup, but one in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine that is mixed. Again, the wording seems to contain a contradiction, for “mixed” and “unmixed” are not at all alike. How, then, can the cup be both unmixed and mixed? For God’s judgment and the discipline that will come upon us are unmixed, and mixed while remaining unmixed. What is mixed? Right judgment with righteousness—not lawlessness, not injustice, nor anything doubtful mixed with righteousness. Rather, it is truly pure and unmixed. The eye of judgment is holy and clear, strong in righteousness and radiant, keen-sighted, precise in its inquiry, upright in its actions, weighing everything, and impartial. Therefore the cup is in the Lord’s hand with unmixed wine, because injustice is not mixed with righteousness. Nor is there anyone among the adversaries who can introduce uncertainty into the judge’s truth, for the cup is in the Lord’s hand with unmixed wine. And if it contains unmixed wine, how can it be full and mixed? Do not think that these words contradict one another; rather, the truth brings them into agreement. The cup is unmixed, as I have said many times, because injustice is not mixed with righteousness; and it is mixed because love for humanity is mixed with righteousness. It is as though he were saying that it is pure in righteousness and mixed with love for humanity, because he shows mercy when he disciplines, and disciplines when he shows mercy.

And see another new principle of truth: it is a sign of God’s care and love for humanity when he disciplines sinners, and a sign of goodness and anger when he does not discipline the offender. Then be afraid [?], as though he hated you and turned his face away when you sinned and he did not discipline you. “The Lord,” he says, “chastises the one he loves; he scourges every son whom he accepts.” From the one whose sins are numerous he turns his face away and leaves him without discipline or punishment. And who makes this clear? God himself, through the prophet: “Because you transgress my laws,” he says, “I will not punish your daughters when they prostitute themselves, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery.” It is as though he were saying, “I will hand you over to your sins. I will not punish injustice, restrain corruption, or heal the wounds of your transgressions, but will allow you to die there in your wickedness.” See how, when he is angry, he threatens not to discipline; and when he truly loves, he does not refrain from discipline.

[?] Now it has been shown, brothers, as far as we are able, what kind of prayer this was and what he wishes to show by saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”: such words come not from his divine majesty but from his human dispensation. The Lord himself made it still clearer that I attribute the humbler words to the weakness of the flesh—to fear, agitation, and sorrow—so that it might be confirmed that he truly assumed flesh capable of suffering. “My spirit,” he says, “is willing, but my flesh is weak.” I repeat [?] the saying many times to establish the understanding of the truth. Then, if anyone dares to set aside the solution to the question that we have given, let him come forward, present himself, and fight against our words, if he is capable of doing battle with the divine word. Let him not [?] like an enemy, but let him fight openly, face to face, like a champion contending for the truth.

But let this be enough for now, for we have returned to our starting point, and there let us bring the discourse to rest. It seems to me that the pattern of the dispensation and the explanation of this saying have been shown fully and completely. For even if someone disputes it after so much testimony, the truth will not thereby be impaired. As Paul also says, “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the churches of God.” For we have learned from the Scriptures to believe, not to chew the cud of speculative inquiry. And I pray to err with [?], rather than to display cleverness with Plato.

Let what has been said be ample and sufficient for us, and let us only remember the poor. Paul fittingly reminded us of this today: “Peter, James, and John gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.” And immediately he added to this, “Only let us remember the poor.” Let us too remember the poor—the poor, so that we may remember ourselves. If you show mercy to another, you show mercy to yourself. You do good to yourself if you do good to the poor. You sow for yourself and reap for yourself. Mercy is sown here, and kindness is reaped in heaven. And do not say, “What can I do? I am bound by poverty. I wish to show mercy, but I am unable. I desire to do good, but my straitened circumstances do not permit it.” Do as much as you can. Perform good deeds to the extent that you are able.

Learn not only to be eager to listen, but also to show mercy, you who are in need. And listen to Isaiah: “Give bread to the hungry with the intention of your heart.” What does “with the intention of your heart” mean? It is another way of saying that if you take from what you yourself would eat and give it, and share your food with the poor person, you have shown mercy to yourself by feeding him. Do you remember? I know that you also remember what was said earlier about mercy. Mercy brings about friendship with God. Mercy brings forgiveness of sins. Mercy delivers from death. Blessed Tabitha, who was handed over to death according to the laws of nature, returned once more from death to life through the gratitude of the widows, for the tears of the poor broke down the gates of death. Pay attention to how much the prayers of the needy can accomplish [?]. When Tabitha, who was full of good deeds, died, all the widows came and stood around Peter, weeping. And the tears of the poor subdued their grief—or rather, overcame the very tyranny of death. For she who had died according to the laws of nature returned again through the word of grace. She was full of mercy and good deeds. The widows wept and moved God to mercy. Dying accords with our nature, but raising the dead is outside and above our nature. So if the tears of the needy could accomplish what is beyond our nature, can they not accomplish what accords with our nature? Consider how powerful a widow’s cries are when she cries out against a rich man. If a poor man cries out against a powerful man who oppresses him, if an orphan cries out against those who deprive him [?], what vengeance will their cries bring about! Let no poor person cry out against you, let no needy person groan, and let no orphan lament and raise a complaint against you. Instead, sow mercy among orphans, so that you may store up kindness for your own children.

Imitate Abraham, who spread the compassion of his love for humanity among all who were in need and left his descendants a pledge of salvation. And see the wonders: because of the honor he showed through hospitality, he was deemed worthy to receive even the angels of God. He received the angels hospitably, thinking they were human beings; afterward he learned that they were angels, and with them he saw God. Because he loved hospitality, God gave him an inexhaustible table in return. For forty years, while the people descended from him lived as strangers in the wilderness, God fed them abundantly, preparing a table for them in the wilderness. He gave his children food produced of itself for forty years in the wilderness and fed the people descended from Abraham because of Abraham’s table of hospitality. And because the shade of his tree refreshed many poor people, a sheltering cloud refreshed the people and carefully preserved the branches sprung from that God-worshiping root. And see the wonders—what a repayment he made! Human beings ate the bread of angels. These were indeed fitting counterparts, for Abraham too received the angels. Because the angels ate [?] belonging to human beings, human beings in turn ate what belonged to angels. For hospitality advances in this way: by receiving human beings, one comes to receive angels too, and from hosting angels, one comes to host God as well. For it was God who had the angels attending him as fellow guests. Thus our Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, when speaking of the fruit of the table of those who love humanity, said, “Whoever receives you receives me.” So the blessed Abraham also received God through his hospitality.

And see the wonders: he saw three, but bowed down to only one. For he did not say “Lords,” but “Lord.” He saw three and blessed the one. But now is not the time to examine this closely; rather, it is time to set forth the teaching about hospitality, since he received them and gave them rest. See the new mysteries of God’s love for humanity, and what debts the Lover of humanity will repay. “I am,” he says, “the God of the fathers, who came down from heaven. You fed the heavenly beings, and I will give heavenly food to your descendants.” Beyond what is natural for angels, angels ate human food; and beyond human nature [?], human beings enjoy heavenly bread. This food is not proper to the nature of angels, nor was that food suited to human nature. But now is not the time to set this forth precisely and [?]. Instead, long for a life of hospitality and undertake the good struggle on behalf of the poor, so that you may store up treasure for yourself. You have the handles of the plow: sow in the fields of the destitute. “He distributed,” it says, “and gave to [?]; his righteousness remains forever.” Let this much suffice. This further reminder concerning the poor was given not as instruction, but as confirmation, for what was said before was already enough to encourage those whose minds are trained.

Let us henceforth attend to our spiritual father, who is the true teacher of the church. Let us too say to him at the appropriate time, “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp,” for we need your teaching and your fatherly voice to confirm these words of ours. Though there is much flour, a little leaven is also needed. Though we have spoken many words, we need your fatherly assistance to uphold and confirm our words, to the glory of Christ our God, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
